1.	Is the government aware of the serious condition of the poultry industry in the province of British Columbia at the present time as a result of the unfair competition of the importation of eggs from the United States ?
2.	Is the government aware that eggs known as "culls" or "small" eggs from the state of Washington are being dumped on the British Columbia market by American producers?
3.	Is the government aware that the duty on eggs into Canada is three cents per dozen whilst duty on eggs into the United States is eight cents per dozen?
4.	Will the government undertake to remedy this unfair competition ?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
causes. The past three years or so have been a period of rapid transition in the poultry business in British Columbia. A few years ago British Columbia was the largest importing province in Canada, from the standpoint of eggs, not only from United States but from the prairies and, earlier, from eastern Canada as well. Latterly, however, production in British Columbia has increased to the point where they not only supply their own requirements but during the winter months practically the total fresh egg requirements of the prairie provinces as well. Further, in addition to shipping to prairie points, British Columbia placed upwards of twenty-five cars of eggs last year in Canada at points east of the Great Lakes.
2.	There is reason to believe that previous to the date imported eggs were included under the egg regulations, (October, 1922) a quantity of small or cull eggs from the states of Washington and Oregon did find their way onto the British Columbia market but since the regulations covering imports became effective, it has been required that the containers of such eggs must be marked with the name of the class and grade when lower than the grade "firsts." The fact that these eggs were marked "seconds" has done a great deal to discourage their import both in British Columbia and in the east.
3.	Yes.
4.	Not by a retaliatory tariff. Some remedy however is now being supplied by more stringent inspection regulations.

speechtext:
1.	Does Thomas Mulvey, Under Secretary of State, draw any salary or remuneration from the government other than his salary as deputy minister?
2.	If so, how much and upon what authority?
3.	How much money has Mr. Mulvey been paid to date in the way of salary or special remuneration other than his salary as deputy minister since 1921?
4.	How much has he drawn in expense account in the years 1921 to 1923 inclusive?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
1.	Mr. Mulvey draws no salary or other remuneration from the government other than his salary as deputy. Certain payments are, however, made to him by the Custodian of Enemy Property, under the following circumstances :
The question of payment to Mr. Mulvey as Deputy Custodian of Enemy Property, was referred by the Right Honourable A. L. Sifton, then Secretary of State, to Messrs. O. M. Biggar and Christopher C. Robinson, the 
legal members of the Enemy Debts Committee. The following is an extract from their report, dated 17th September, 1920:
Mr. Mulvey's work has extended over a period of about four and a half years, and in our opinion an extra allowance at the rate of $1,500 a year, or a total of $6,750, would be a small recompense for the special services rendered.
Payment of $4,000 was made to Mr. Mulvey by direction of an order in council dated 17th December, 1921, P.C. 4,631. Subsequently the balance of the amount, at the rate aforesaid, was paid to Mr. Mulvey by the Custodian.
2.	Payment has been made at the rate of $125 a month out of commissions earned by the Custodian's Office, upon the direction of the Custodian. The authority to make this payment was under consideration by the Department of Justice, and the following is taken from an opinion of that department, dated 30th January, 1924:
The expense of getting in, liquidating, and otherwise dealing with property, rights and interests, seeing that the government is only required to account for the "net proceeds" of such property, rights and interests, may be defrayed, on the order of the Custodian, out of any profits which may be earned in dealing with the same.
3.	Mr. Mulvey has been paid the balance accruing up to the 1st January, 1922, $4,500 and $125 per month since that time, out of commissions earned by the Custodian's office.
4.	Expense account 1921, including travelling expenses to London, Paris, Brussels and Berlin, and the reception of His Excellency the Governor General, amounted to $2,052.30, paid out of appropriation "Demobilization" and contingencies.
Expense account 1922, including travelling expenses to London, Brussels, Amsterdam, Hamburg, Berlin, Prague, Vienna, Budapest, Paris, Metz, Strasbourg and Zurich, amounted to $3,249.38 paid out of appropriation "Adjustment of War Claims." Less $250 paid out of contingencies.
Expense account 1923, including travelling expenses to London, Paris, Brussels and Washington, amounted to $1,914, paid out of commissions earned by Custodian's office.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.
Department of the Interior-Scientific institutions- Expenses connected with the Dominion Observatory Ottawa, $50,000.
Expenses connected with the Dominion Astrophysical Observatory at Victoria, B.C., $18,500.
Would the minister explain the particulars of these votes?

speakeroldname: Hon. CHARLES STEWART (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The scientific institutions referred to are the observatories both in Ottawa and in Victoria. They carry on astro-physical and astronomical research work. That is about the extent of the explanation that I can give, except to present a list of the names of the men who are engaged in the work, compiling data for scientific purposes, as well as adjusting the time, taken from observations of the sun, which is now practically the universal time throughout Canada. I confess that as a layman I find it rather difficult to enter into any detailed description of the work carried on at these two institutions.
I notice there is a decrease in the vote for the Ottawa Observatory, but none in the case of the institution at Victoria.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is explained by the nature of the work under way in British Columbia. It was felt that to get the full benefit of the investigations which Dr. Plaskett is carrying on at Victoria some further outlay for an addition to the building and the provision of supplies was necessary.
Can we get some details as to this expenditure at Victoria?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The service under this head for which money is to be expended is as follows:

There is a difference of $8,420, reduction apparently on the first item. The last item is the same. How is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The observatory of British Columbia is exactly the same, and we were able to make a slight cut here.
What has been dispensed with? Where is the cut?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Largely on supplies. Our staff is the same. 'We do not require the same amount of supplies as we did formerly.

Can we have the
details of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
give my hon. friend the cut. It is taken off the supplies. We allow the same amount as last year for Victoria, but in the case of Ottawa it is a cut all along the line of small amounts out of supplies, not off the salary.
Is it the general supplies?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Then there is this difference between the amount of supplies

purchased last year and the amount proposed to be purchased this year. Was there an unusual supply purchased last year, or just the ordinary amount?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I cannot say what the difference would be between last year and the year before.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: This vote used to run about $30,000 a year, but I observe that in 1922 it took a sudden increase, and the increase continued, and last year was the highest $58,000. Is the sudden increase for 1922 estimate due to the installation of the observatory at Victoria? If not, why can the amount not be brought back to the original average of about $30,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
answer that question, I fear. I do not know if there was any increase. My hon. friend has asked why we should not go back to the original vote now that the observatory is established at Victoria. There was no appreciable drop, because the work at Victoria-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: My hon. friend missed my point. When was the Victoria observatory established? When was the first increase in the vote due to the establishment of that observatory?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Then, long after 1918, for example in 1921; the estimate was $31,000, and then there was an estimate of, I think, $40,000 odd for the following year, or perhaps $50,000, and last year $58,000. What I do not understand is why we cannot get back to the estimate that we had even after the Victoria observatory was built?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I was not aware that there was any increase. I have not looked into the estimates of 1921.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I have them here.
Why was this observatory instituted at Victoria, instead of some othet part of Canada? What function did it perform there?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
answer my hon. friend in regard to that. That was established before my time.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
You can see better from Victoria, I believe, than from any other part of Canada for observatory purposes. I believe for every other purpose you can see pretty well there.

Supply-Interior
Will the minister explain how they can run the observatoiy at Victoria for $18,500 when it takes some $50,000 to run the observatory at Ottawa?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think that would be very easily answered. It is because they do not attempt anything like the amount of work at Victoria that is being done at Ottawa.

Can the minister explain it any' more in detail, I would like to find out the difference. As I understand it, in Victoria they have one of the largest telescopes in the world. They are doing better work and getting more satisfactory results than are obtained almost anywhere on this continent. If the object of the observatory is to look at the stars, and you have the largest telescope in Victoria, why are the results there not to be compared with the results here, and why should the observatory at Ottawa cost so much money?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon.
member is probably quite correct, the best telescope is undoubtedly in the coast, and perhaps the atmospheric conditions lend themselves more acceptably to observation out there. My hon. friend must remember that telescopic observation is not the only work that is being carried on at Ottawa. That is being carried on as well, true not with as strong an instrument, but they are carrying on a great many other scientific observations at Ottawa.

That is what I was
asking.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Namely photographing sun spots with very intricate instruments.

That is done with a
telescope.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
How is it done?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Scientifically I cannot explain it. It is done with a telescope, but not the kind of telescope in use at Victoria or Vancouver.

They are making
photographs out there?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Playing with the sun
spots all the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If you want all the scientific information, I am afraid you
will hardly get it from me. I do not pretend to be a scientist, but I know they are carrying on a great deal more scientific work, at the parent institution at Ottawa than at Victoria. They are only making a start at Victoria, and undoubtedly, if further work is to be undertaken, a great deal more money will require to be spent there. There is no question about the value of the work Dr. Plaskett is carrying on. Dr. Klotz established in Ottawa instruments for measuring earthquakes. The locality of these earthquakes can be measured almost within a few miles. They have numberless instruments for various scientific purposes, and men competent to handle them. Naturally you will have a greater expense at Ottawa than at Victoria.
There is a seismograph at Victoria?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is
a small one. We have a very accurate one in Ottawa. Indeed, I think we had the most accurate information registered at Ottawa in regard to the earthquakes in Japan.
That would not make up this extra amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
make that claim for a moment. I did not make that assertion.

The information we
have from the minister is certainly very general and he must have some further details. So far, we have the photographing of sun spots and the measuring of earthquakes. Those two operating will not make up this difference.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I would
not say that they would.
I think we are entitled to some further information.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The minister may not
know very much about the scientific phase of this matter, but I want to impress upon him the financial phase. In 1918-19, the estimate for this item was $25,000; in 1919-20; $31,000; in 1920-21, $36,000; in 1921-22, $50,715; then the minister's estimate for last year was $58,000, and his estimate for this year is $55,000. The increase, it will be seen, took place some considerable time after the Victoria Observatory 4 p.m. was established. I know good work is being done, that is if you describe good work as excellent work from the scientific standpoint. I do not know any other branch of the Interior de-
Supply-Interior

partment which contains more highly technical men and men more devoted to their task than does the observatory. Some of the best mathematicians of our country are there. At least when Dr. Klotz was head, the enthusiasm of the branch knew no bounds; it certainly would have known no financial bound if he had had his way. What I want to impress upon the minister is this, that, while we must, I think, maintain observatories and do certain work that is supposed to be one of the functions of nationhood, and, while I do not think it would do for Canada to be without such an institution, nevertheless, the highest scientific phases are really for our universities and they would better be done there. I would be sorry to see an extension of the government's functions into all these scientific fields, building them up to an elaborate degree. The minister's face should be turned the other way, and we ought to try to get back to a $30,000 estimate in this matter. We cannot do that in one year, but I do not think the minister should ask parliament for any more than what he asked for t'he year before last. Let him take off last year's increase and go back to the $50,000 estimate. That would be a good start. It is not that I decry the work, I would like to encourage it if I could; but if we take the line of economy, undoubtedly we ought to keep to that line in this case.
Is it proposed to reduce the staff at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We are
pressing very hard for reductions all round. As regards scientific institutions of this character, the work of which is undoubtedly very valuable, it is hard to tell just how far we should cut this service. A layman, who may be more familiar with other services, can form a better judgment as to the real necessities of the country in connection with them. While we are all agreed as to the real necessity of this for the country, it is doubtful how far the work should go; but the government is willing, in this and every other expenditure, to cut them as far as it is possible to do so without seriously interfering with the services.
There is no reduction in the staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not that I am aware of.
Would it not be possible to reduce the staff?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There are
a number who are due for retirement. Dr. Klotz died just recently.

Has anybody been put
in his place?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not yet.

Is it intended to do so?
Mr. STEWART (Argenteuil) r Yes. There must be a director.

Could someone not be
promoted?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. It is
not the intention to increase any staff where we can get along without doing so. Where deaths or superannuations occur, vacancies will be filled from positions below them, if at all possible.

And then some person
appointed below to fill that vacancy?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Then, is that not a position that should not be filled, if it is intended to reduce the staff wherever possible?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There
would be a reduction of one. There must be a director to take the place of Dr. Klotz, but that would be a promotion.

I observe that
in 1921 there was a vote of $10,200 for the Victoria office. In 1921, supplies were as high, if not higher in some instances, than they are now, and the cost of living was much about the same, so that salaries should be about the same. We have had an increase of a little over eighty per cent in running that one institution in that comparatively short time. The cost has increased from $10,200 in the last three years to $18,500. Is that an increase in number of men on the staff, new machinery, new instruments-or what?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There have been two additional appointments-an assistant astronomer to Dr. Plaskett at $1,800, and an instrument maker foreman, at $1,860. Those men are also granted house allowances as the observatory is not yet completed.
Do I understand that the appointment of those two men means an additional $8,300?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

How is the increase accounted for? I have only two extra men so far.

Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
tell my hon. friend what the increased expenses would be. But I do not think the expenses are high. They include instruments, 31,800; photographic supplies, $500; machine and instrument work, $600; hardware and chemicals, $400:	automobile maintenance,
$500; postage, freight and telephone, $600; contingencies, $400. I understand that these men have to live in Victoria, and have to travel some considerable distance between the observatory and the city.
Does the minister mean the two recent appointees?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, the
whole staff-I am wrong. Dr. Plaskett lives there.

To what extent do
unfavourable climatic conditions interfere with the work of the observatory at Victoria?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot
say that unfavourable climatic conditions prevail at Victoria for work of this character.

Mr. Chairman, I might
say that after a very careful examination of all suggested points in Canada, this site, about eight miles out from Victoria, was selected on account of the clearness of the atmosphere and for other reasons favourable to this particular kind of work.

I spent a couple of
winter months in Victoria three years ago, and during that period I am quite certain there was no time when observations could be carried out. It is my impression that throughout the winter months it would be very difficult to carry on observatory work there.
The weather has been ideal ever since.

As vacancies occur in
the natural order of things does the minister propose to dimmish the staff by not making further appointments?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, whenever possible there will not be additions made; rather reductions.

What was the
amount spent last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
When I first took charge of the department I reduced the vote because I had not a complete return, and I found myself short at the end of the year. Last session, Mr. Chairman, a great deal of unmerited criticism was indulged in at the expense of the surveys branch. Of this criticism the most unmerited was directed at the topographical work carried on by that branch of the Dominion Lands department. In my humble opinion, no survey work carried on by any governmental body has a higher economic value than well executed topographical surveys. The amount of misinformation about our country and its resources is directly in proportion to our lack of topographical maps. We have had surveys at a greater cost per head of the population than in almost any other country, this being due to the division of authority between the Dominion and the provinces, and the lack of a properly coordinated scheme of surveys and map making based on scientific principles. At present the geological survey produces magnificent maps as a basis for geological and mineral investigations. Unfortunately their operations are too restricted to be at all adequate. The Department of National Defence is also making increasingly splendid maps which are even more valuable to the civil than to military. authorities. The Topographical Surveys branch of the Interior department has been making maps of what was originally Dominion lands. But Dominion responsibility goes beyond Dominion lands, it extends to all the provinces, and Dominion aid towards mapping should be granted adequately to all of the provinces. The Dominion government has spent nearly thirty millions of dollars in the western provinces since 1900, part of this money being spent not on 70
Dominion lands but on private property. I claim that other provinces have the right to their share of that expenditure. The western provinces have been treated fairly. There have been expended on geodetic surveys $871,581, on topographical surveys $15,717,524, and on base lines, meridian lines, township outlines, and section outlines $11,554,277. As far as I am concerned I see no reason why the money voted for topographical surveys should not be divided in proportion to the area of each province. At present I understand that the topographical surveys branch contemplates extending its work to Quebec and the Maritime provinces. That work is undoubtedly needed, and I would suggest to the minister that it should be undertaken after consulting with the provinces concerned. I would also suggest to the minister that the amount voted for geodetic surveys is not sufficient for provincial requirements. Splendid work is being done for the provinces at the present time, but money now spent in the extension of operation will save millions of dollars to the provinces in the years to come by providing the permanent framework for mapping, without which mudh other survey work would have to be repeated over and over again.
May I add for the information of the minister that the functions for each branch should be more definitely specified, and that a well qualified engineer or land surveyor should be attached to the deputy minister's office in a consulting capacity. This man would see that duplication and overlapping would not occur. I should be sorry if my remarks were considered as an attack upon the land surveyors of the Dominion. They have done their work fairly, and they are entitled to the congratulations of this House for what they have accomplished for the country. I am very sorry to see a decrease in these estimates when the government desires to carry out the development of our natural resources. I also wish to advise the minister that it would be a great mistake to dismiss any of these officials who are trained in practical work, and whose capacity and energy are not surpassed in any other country in the world.

On photo topographical surveys we have one party; classification of lands, four parties. In British Columbia the whole of the topographical surveys are carried on. Supervision and inspection costs us $2,000 in Manitoba, $2,000 in Saskatchewan and $3,000 in Alberta, and " unprovided for " we have appropriations for each province of a small amount. That means 29 parties all told.
In reply to my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown), we have ceased projecting surveys. There is no work being done on the meridian and base line.

The subject of surveys is undoubtedly a very important matter, but, as far as I can observe, in the estimates it has not been overlooked from a financial point of view. I notice in vote No. 97 there is provision for $35,000 for topographic surveys under National Defence department, which represents a reduction from Jast year of some $10,000. Just what the value of a survey of that character, as distinguished from a topographic survey is, I am sure I am at a loss to understand. Then we have vote No. 251, the one under consideration, $470,000; and we have the Geodetic survey, vote No. 252, which represents $275,000. Then I find Geological survey, item 268, representing an amount of $320,000. Then we have another variety of survey shown at page 56 of the estimates under Dominion lands and parks, as follows:
For surveys and investigations of water and power resources, including the Dominion Hydrometric survey for the reclamation of lands by irrigation and drainage and for the administration of the Acts in connection therewith, and so forth, $547,000.
Now these surveys I take it, Mr. Chairman, are all necessarily inter-related, so that one is more or less dependent upon the other, and I certainly think that the minister should make a representation to his department to have this work in some way or other put under one head, who would be responsible for it, thereby I am sure lessening expense. I would suggest also that he should in addition impress upon his colleague of the

National Defence department the necessity for eliminating that survey for militia purposes altogether. In my judgment, so far as I can observe, it is more or less a useless expenditure. It ought to be, it seems to me, a comparatively easy task to, shall I use the word, co-ordinate, this work? Surely it is not beyond the capacity of the officials of the Interior department to get together and prepare that work and relate it, so that a great deal of this expense, considerably over a million dollars, might be saved. If the officials of the Interior department and the officials of the other department are not able to do that, I would suggest that they should call in the services of the Civil Service Commission-and I am sure the minister would have no objection to that-and ask them to undertake the work of trying to make these various organizations work together, and eliminate, I am sure, a very large proportion of the expense involved in these services. It seems to me that it is in this direction that savings can be made. Economy does not consist in simply eliminating a certain percentage of employees here or there, it must be carried on in a scientific and proper manner. I certainly am disappointed that the vote this year for these various services represents such a substantial amount. It seems to me it should be substantially reduced. We can if necessary eliminate much survey work during the next two or three years at least, because after all what we all desire, and what the people of Canada demand, is the strictest possible economy.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is costing
the services of a survey party, probably five or six or seven thousand dollars. That is the average cost of a party for a season.

Shall we put
down $5,000 as the cost of the Survey of Jasper?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not
know. The party would not be detailed all summer at Jasper.

I take it that
my hon. friend cannot give any real information as to that. Topographical and general surveys,-that represents a class of work by itself. How much of this $470,000 is for topographical and general surveys?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
General
and miscellaneous, $23,450; topographical, $48,000; photo-topographical, $4,500.

What is the
allowance for traverse of northern rivers and lakes?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
How much for
classification of lands for the settlement and development of Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
How much for
plotting and printing of plans?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
$13,600 for
printing and stationery, and lithographing, $12,500.

If I have got
my hon. friend down right he has accounted for $148,000 out of the vote of $470,000. That is right?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Then the whole of the balance is behind the "etc."

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There is
nothing strange about it.

What is it,
though?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We spent
in Manitoba, $24,450; in Saskatchewan-
What for?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I beg my
hon. friend's pardon. The salaries for the permanent staff amount to $170,260; office employees at Ottawa, $68,340; interprovincial boundary, $3,000; western levelling, $9,590; soils, $3,100; warehouse, $1,060-making a total of $255,350. Now, if my hon. friend will take the balance: head office printing and Stationery, $13,600; purchase and repair of instruments, $7,000; lithographing, etc., $12,500; equipment, $8,000; western soils, $300; western warehouse, $300-he will get a total of $41,700.

Supply-Interior

Why does the
minister ask for more than the total on his own showing?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Perhaps
my hon. friend will check his first list. Here are details of that expenditure:	Manitoba,
$24,450; Saskatchewan, $40,500; Alberta, $44,500; British Columbia, $8,500; Quebec, $9,000; Maritime provinces, $26,000; Yukon territory, $3,000; Northwest territories, $10,000; Alberta and British Columbia boundary $7,000-making a total of $172,950.
That is a different calculation altogether; they cannot both be right.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am giving my hon. friend the details. I answered the question in his first item.

Yes; then I
asked for everything that "etc" covered. The hon. minister gave me that and said it made a total of $41,700. Now he has some [DOT] other particulars.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, I have
given my hon. friend the exact figures making up that amount. Those figures which I have given to my hon. friend total $470,000.

I am afraid I cannot check the figures, nor do I think any member of this committee has been able to check them. However that may be, does the minister really think that any harm would follow if all the work for the traversing of northern rivers and lakes stopped this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
What?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Navigation
has become a very important factor there.
Where?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On the Mackenzie river. My hon. friend knows that three transportation companies are doing business on that river.
What work is proposed to be done there now?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Simply traversing the river and doing the necessary work to make it reasonably safe.
Does this apply to one river?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Part of the work is on the Great Slave lake, but it is all in contiguous territory. I am wrong. There is some work to be done at Le Pas, northern Manitoba, in the mining district.

Reference has been made to the disparity between the expenditures in the various provinces. In the case of Saskatchewan, can the minister tell us what part of the expenditure has been on lands forming part of the natural resources which have not been turned over to the province?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the only amount would be $5,500 for the re-establishment of monuments in the areas where they have been obliterated. The balance is all in the areas that are purely and simply Crown lands of the federal government.
Are we to understand that if the natural resources had been turned over to the province, the expenditure under this item would be only $5,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would be $5,500.

Mr. Chairman, the vote provides for classification of lands for settlement. I have seen some of the work and I think it is excellent. The information gained by this classification will be very useful if it ever gets to the right quarter; but it will be of very little value if buried in the archives of the department. What efforts are being made by the department to have the information printed on maps in the languages of the various countries from which the minister is soliciting settlers? For example, a Pole goes into an immigration office at Dantzig; he is told a great deal about this country he wants to know from the agent just where he should settle; the agent paints a glowing picture, assisted by Canadian Pacific propaganda and other colonization propaganda, of the great opportunities for farming in Canada; but the man is not quite sure that things are as rosy as the agent paints them; thereupon the agent takes him over to the classification map and directs his attention to the nice colouring. But the Pole cannot be sure that everything is as pictured by the immigration agent, and we know that the latter is not always above suspicion. I suggest the language of the countries from which we expect immigrants be used on maps of this kind, when sent abroad.
I fully support the statements of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw). I think the expenditures on surveys in all the various departments is very close to a Teapot Dome scandal. Let me add a few more of these surveys that we have discovered in running through the estimates:	Department of
National Defence, topographical surveys, $35,000; then item 251-the one we are now considering-topographical surveys of the Depart-
Supply-Interior

ment of the Interior, $470,000; geodetic survey of Canada, item 252, $275,000; geological survey, item 268, $320,000; for surveys and investigations of water and power resources, page 56, $547,000; these sums total about $1,647,000. But in the moment that elapsed between questions and some explanations by the minister we found, on page 53, that Indians are taken care of in the way of surveys-$8,000 for Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, $52,250 for British Columbia and $3,000 for general, or a grand total spent by this government on surveys in Canada of $1,710,250. The intentions of the minister regarding co-ordination and economy may be excellent, but the lower regions, we are told are paved with good intentions.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is very kind of my hon. friend to say that the lower regions are paved with good intentions, but so are some of the upper regions.

May I conclude before the minister replies to my question? I submit that the minister might take into more serious consideration the recommendations made last year, the year before, and this year with respect to coordination of all those surveys. The public expects that there should be quick action, not next year or the year after, but at once.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Is my hon.
friend through? I may tell him that the minister has no intention of reducing the geological survey by one party or one dollar. In view of the fact that we are gaining rapidly in mineral production I think this is the most important piece of survey work that can be done in Canada. My hon. friend smiles; let him look at the records and discover how much the mineral production of Canada has increased in the last few years.

The minister will surely forgive me; I was not smiling at the suggestion that this vote was important, but rather at the implication that I suggested for a moment he should reduce this particular item. I have pointed out that $1,710,000 odd is to be spent on various surveys, and I submit that the adoption of the recommendation of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) that there be amalgamation or coordination-anything you like to call it-of the various survey departments, would indubitably lead to economies that would be effective in reducing the total expenditure under this head.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, and the expenditure is reduced this year by $100,000;

my hon. friend has missed that small item in his calculations. I repeat what I said a few moments ago, that there is co-ordinated effort. I have said that it was my desire to see the topographical work all under one head; I have repeated that half a dozen times. Now my hon. friend has mentioned that we have suryeys in the Indian department. We have one surveyor in that department. We are trying to complete, with the province of British Columbia, the work in connection with what has been a vexed question ever since confederation, namely, the allocation of Indian reserves. Considerable additions to the reserves have been granted to British Columbia for this purpose, largely the outcome of the work of a commission appointed to deal with the matter. Hon. gentlemen who have been in office will remember that this was a very serious question, and it is not yet settled. When these reserves are properly set apart they will have to be surveyed, and the item appears on these estimates for that particular purpose. So my hon. friend has not discovered any mare's nest or any Teapot Dome. There is not a cent in any of these items the expenditure of which is not justified in the interests of Canada. While we could do without some of the work-quite properly so -I have pointed out that there has been a reduction of $100,000, which I regard as a respectable reduction under this head, and everything we are asking for is required, particularly the items in connection with the work to precede the geological survey. My hon. friend knows that you cannot send a geological survey party out to make a reconnaissance without having the topographical work precede it, and a very large proportion of this item is for work of this character. As to overlapping, I have said repeatedly that there is none. I have been very frank with the committee; I have nothing to hide. But it naturally incenses one when mention is made of Teapot Dome or any other kind of dome in connection with a vote of this character, and I propose to defend the vote somewhat heatedly.

The hon. minister seemed
to be a little heated over the Teapot Dome allusion, but I do not think he need take that very seriously; I think it just came in as an afterthought on the part of the hon. member who was making the suggestions. But in listening to the discussions in regard to the estimates I am struck with the hopelessness of any attempt to get anything lower than just what stands on the books here. I will guarantee that at this stage of the proceedings every minister who comes before the

Supply-Interior
House will defend every item in his estimates as absolutely necessary and will contend that nothing can be done a dollar cheaper. All over this country to-day there is a cry for economy; there is the suggestion that it is costing too much to run the country and that expenditures must be reduced. But it seems almost hopeless for a private member to get up and say anything about the estimates. I cannot see anything else for it but to keep pegging away.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no objection to any questions or any suggestions that may be made, but I do object to references of the character indulged in by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) concerning the men who are in this department or concerning my administration.
Will the minister answer my question about what is intended regarding the classification of land and the maps that are sent out based thereon?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, with
pleasure. There are no maps sent abroad of the character he mentions. The information is in our land offices at Prince Albert, Edmonton. Calgary or wherever the work is being carried on, and it is available to the prospective settler. Only a comparatively small area has been covered as yet, but so far as the work has gone I think the results speak for themselves and that they are appreciated by the people. As for sending maps abroad, I had some experience in the Immigration department. My hon. friend has criticized the propaganda sent out to various countries to encourage settlement in Canada. Perhaps those statements are too glowing; I am prepared to agree with my hon. friend. I think also that other organizations outside the control of the government do paint very glowing pictures, at least if one is to judge by the statements made by settlers who have come to Canada. But so far as I am concerned I have warned every officer with whom I came in contact to tell the whole truth; that the truth was good enough; that the facts could be stated with respect to lands and opportunities in Canada and the people concerned could then make up their own minds about it. I am not going to suggest that I would like information of that sort to go abroad. I think it is well to have it in the land offices, available for anyone who goes there-and they must go there in order to secure maps and diagrams of the localities in which they propose to settle. These prospective settlers,
no matter what country they come from, are usually accompanied by a friend who can speak the language and who knows the kind of information that is given out.

The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) tells us that no matter what is said or done by any private member' the amounts brought down by the minister will go through, and we have a cry of despair from the hon. gentleman because of the impossibility, as he says, of doing anything about it. But I would tell him that it is not at all impossible if members are really serious in their cries for economy, and if they have not only the courage to talk but also the courage to vote accordingly. It is not at all impossible to do, and usefully do, a good deal. We have had votes on the question of economy. We have had votes, for example, on the question of $50,000 for ornamental lighting and the like. We have had loud declamations against extravagance. We have had them here. The hon. gentleman says it is no use. Well, if he has the courage of his convictions-
I have had the courage of my convictions.

Then I will give the hon. gentleman an opportunity now by moving a reduction in this vote of $65,450, and I point out the grounds on which that motion is absolutely in order, having regard to the statement of the. minister himself. I take the first line "Topographical and general surveys." The alleged justification for this work at the present time is in connection with the all important geological surveys, and we have had the admission this afternoon that this work was well ahead of the geological work and was not necessary for that purpose. I therefore move to reduce the vote by these two items together, one of $46,000, and the other of $23,450, making $69,450.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Do I understand that my hon. friend is proposing to reduce the vote for topographical surveys to $60,000?
No. I purposely made it a very, very reasonable reduction, following the minister's explanation. I moved to reduce it by the sum of $69,450.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not understand how my hon. friend arrives at his deductions. I may say that we have a large number of requests from various sources for topographical survey work, and I think in fairness to myself and to the committee I should say that these amounts have been cut,
Supply-Interior

and very heavily cut, from the appropriations first presented to me. I had felt that I was making a very substantial reduction. After going at the thing, not with the idea of giving all the service that I thought was desired, but rather cutting it as far as I could, almost to the minimum, I have made a cut in the two services of $100,000, which I think is a fairly respectable cut, having in mind the service to be rendered. I am prepared to say that next year I can come with a further substantial reduction. I have reduced every year since I have been minister. I have tried to meet the conditions that I think exist in the country; I have tried to be economical in my department, but my hon. friend is never satisfied, nor would he be satisfied if I cut the vote by $100,000 more. If I cut it down by that amount he would still take the ground he is taking now, that it ought to be cut some more. There has never been a year in which my hon. friend has not treated this vote in the very same way. I have no quarrel with reduction. I am trying to reduce. ' My hon, friend should bear in mind that this service was not inaugurated as a war service. It was part of the general service of the government of which my hon. friend was a member, He thought in his day as minister that it was advisable to carry on this work, but now when another government is in office, and another minister in charge, no matter how big a reduction is made, he wants a still further cut. To be candid with the committee, I felt that I was doing a pretty fair amount of cutting this year. I told the committee last year I would cut, and I have come back this year and kept my promise. I tell the committee again this year that I intend to make a further cut next year. I have told the committee frankly what I think we should get down to in topographical survey work in Canada, and all the other items of survey work.
Let me say one word more with respect to the surveys of the Indian reserves in British Columbia. The matter is not settled at the moment, but we hope that it will be. It has been a very vexatious question, and I think we ought to settle it if it is humanly possible to do so, and have the surveys made, in order that the natives who have spent a great deal of money agitating over this question may settle down upon the reserves allocated to them.
I hope the committee will sustain me in this vote. I think I am safe in saying that I have made a cut in every item in the estimates of the Interior department, and I do not say that I have yet reached the end. I have closed up this year at Saskatoon an office with all the staff. I have made heavy reductions through-

out the department, in order to meet the situation as I see it in Canada at the present time and save some money. I am not administering a department that grew out of war activities.
Will the minister tell us from what sources demands are coming for topographical survey work at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These requests come from practically all the governments except Ontario. Requests for surveys come frequently to our office. We will not be able to give British Columbia anything like what she wishes for this year, and what I think perhaps she is entitled to. So far as the prairie provinces are concerned, I am bound to admit that some division work is away beyond the necessities of the case. As to the other work, that of land classification, in some of the older settled parts, we have to establish lines that have been obliterated. I may say that thousands of requests have been turned down because I felt that we did not have money enough to go on with this work.
I want to thank the minister for the lecture he has been good enough to read me on my rashness in endeavouring to save a little of the country's money at the present time.
Too late.

Of course, that is the cry-too late. This government is so confident of this House that it is too late to challenge a vote when it comes to the House if the government has seen fit to put its imprimatur on it. However, this is absolutely correct. My hon. friend said I was against this vote two years ago. I was. I have always been against it. I think our expenses to-day are ridiculous; they were before, and to the extent that they were higher before they were more ridiculous; but with this difference, unless you are going to go over the lines again you have to come to an end even of surveys. Just imagine anyone seriously objecting to the House trying to bring into effect a little economy at the present time, and yet the minister in charge of this department is running lines up into the arctic circle on the one hand-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend will correct his last statement about running lines to the arctic circle. We are not running lines into the arctic circle but only along the Mackenzie river.

That is the line I am referring to, and it is the one that

Supply-Interior
has been spoken of this afternoon. And then we have the survey of unnecessary divisions and subdivisions in the prairie provinces. If ever there was an admitted case for economy it is here; if there ever was a situation where the government could exercise economy it is in. the present instance.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I may tell my hon. friend that no subdivision work in the prairies is provided for in this vote, not to the extent of one acre.

While compliments are being exchanged across the floor of the House I also wish to thank the hon. member (Sir Henry Drayton) for the lecture he gave me. I think, perhaps, that in doing what he did the hon. member was of opinion he was giving me a " dare." Let me tell my hon. friend that I am not to be influenced in any position I take by any such suggestion. No " dare " of that kind is likely to make any change in the way I shall vote. I can sympathize with the minister in his efforts to get these estimates through.
Hear, hear.
Hon. gentlemen to my right say "Hear, hear." They are always looking for trouble.
We are trying to help the minister.

That is a good spirit to display, I hope my hon. friends will continue it. In estimating for expenditures it is sometimes a good idea to fix a certain sum and make the provision for your necessities come within that figure. If we simply look at the necessities to be met we shall never accomplish any real economy in public expenditures at the present time. This vote is a pretty large one and, notwithstanding what the minister says, I know it is not absolutely required. I can understand that there are conditions which may seem to make the expenditure necessary, but the country will still go on and do very well if a reduction in the sum asked for is made. I am in favour of a reduction not because any " dare " has been extended to me, but because I believe it would be in the public interest.
Think of your conscience.

The hon. gentleman need
not remind me of my conscience, it is quite clear.

Did I understand the
minister to say that the classification of land for settlement was all done on lands belonging to the Crown?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, some
of it is not done. We could render splendid service to many communities but we cannot afford it. There have been a number of new cornel's arriving in Canada, and the object of this classification work has been with a view to getting information for such persons who must depend upon that information in the selection of their land. I cannot promise that expenditure could be made for carrying out surveys of lands already settled. I think for the time being our efforts will have to be confined to the class of work indicated.

Will the minister
state how far these Crown lands are from railway communication?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I might
mention one instance where the classification has taken place in a district my hon. friend is well acquainted with, west of Wetaskiwin and where at the moment the settlers are a considerable distance away from railway communication on the Canadian Pacific. But a line is being run from Lacombe into the territory west of Wetaskiwin. A considerable amount of classification has been done in that territory in which many settlers have located. We find settlers squatted all over; a newcomer who has taken up homestead land does not pay very much attention at first to the railway facilities that exist. I am told that practically all our classification has been confined as far as possible to within fifteen miles of an existing railway.

May I suggest to the
minister that it would be advisable not only to keep classification to districts very close to the railroad, but also to have lands made available for settlement within reasonable distance of the railway lines. If we allow settlers to spread all over the territory we will be called upon to provide transportation facilities for them, facilities that at present we cannot afford.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think I
can agree thoroughly with my hon. friend because that is a policy I have always advocated. Unfortunately it is a very difficult policy to carry put. For example people went into the Peace river district, hundreds of miles from railway facilities, and it cost the country a very considerable amount to extend the railway communication into that country. It must not be understood that I
Supply-Interior

am objecting in any way to the Peace river country itself, it is one of the finest territories that I know of. I simply cited that as a case of a territory into which people were determined to enter and settle. You are not able to prevent settlers from entering certain districts when they conceive a particular fancy for settling there.

I would suggest to the minister the possibility of withdrawing such lands from settlement, because so long as they are made available for that purpose it is natural for people to go there who feel so disposed. I think the time has come when the policy of the government should be to make lands available that are close to transportation facilities, or are in districts that are going to be provided with such facilities in the near future.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Then we
have this other difficulty: Take Fort Vermilion, or the area down at Fort McKay; squatters have settled there and application has been made to have the land surveyed, but we have not granted it. Still, people go in and squat on the land. In this way you have a very difficult proposition to meet and provide for. Knowing the western situation nobody would be happier than I to prevent the indiscriminate spreading of settlement if it were possible, because I am aware of the difficulties that follow.

I will make another
suggestion to the minister and to the government. Possibly the best way to get over this unfortunate situation is for the Dominion to transfer these natural resources to the provinces which can handle them more easily than we can.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am perfectly willing-
"Barkis is willin'".

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: -and always have been.
What has been done with regard to the classification of land in the Peace river country?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am informed that that work was done two years ago for the Soldier Settlement Board, although it was not all our survey work. We do not want to claim all the credit for everything that has been done in this connection. Because as my hon. friend knows, under the Soldiers' Settlement grant, surveys were made

which are probably just as accurate and reliable as those of our engineers. However, there is undoubtedly a very large unsettled area up there as to which accurate information has been filed.

I think.the surveys
extending out into the Peace river country offer a very good example of the system of locating settlers in advance of transportation facilities, and I maintain that if the government surveys the land and throws it open foi settlement they are under an obligation to provide railway facilities for the settlers that come in. Two years ago I pointed out to the minister the danger of surveying land for settlement a long distance from railway facilities. In a short time we shall have settlements grow up in such districts and a demand will be made for branch lines of railway. Then we shall have the same old problem over again that we are now facing of making provision for building these railways. The branch lines that are demanded in the West to-day originated, to a large extent, on account of the oversurvey that was carried out by the government. Wt have a very small population occupying a tremendous tract of territory, and it seems to me that the time has come to stop this reaching out and occupying land beyond transportation facilities.
I was rather surprised to see that the minister intended confining the surveys entirely to crown lands, because from what I know of western Canada there is very little crown land that will be accepted for settlement, unless more railways are built in the West. I live in one of the choicest homestead districts perhaps in western Canada, and yet there is hardly a homestead available there that would be taken up by any settler. Sometimes a man will, in a moment of optimism, and perhaps primed up with colonization literature, file on one of the homesteads, but after a year or two, or possibly in a few months, that man will abandon the homestead pull up stakes and leave, after having done a good deal of hard work and spent considerable money. I think the time has come to stop this practice. We should try and induce settlement near the railways where we have transportation facilities, roads, schools, churches, elevators and all the necessary trade facilities. Let us try and use these. One of the troubles in western Canada is that we are over built. We have too many facilities. Let us try and use what we have before we reach out and demand more.

Supply-Interior

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am sorry
my hon. friend misunderstood me. It was not the survey work; it was the classification work.

I understood the hon.
minister to say the classification for settlement was entirely confined to crown lands.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, it has
not been in the past; but I made the statement that for the future we are cutting down, and we will have to cut down even more than we are doing now. We cannot promise that we will make surveys of areas in which settlement has already taken place, unless there be crown lands for settlement in that area. Then in every case we would be quite willing to do so; but for the federal government to make a survey of all the lands in the hands of private people would be a pretty large undertaking.

Has the minister
considered any claim for forcing the lands now being held by private individuals into use? Throughout the entire western country there are millions of acres of lands adjacent to the railway that are held out of use. The maintenance of railway facilities, the necessity for general development, municipal administration, schools and so on entails a tremendously heavy burden on the settlers who are there. It seems to me the time has come when the government should devise some means of insisting that lands that were intended for bona fide settlers should in some way be restored to the people and made available for use.
Will the hon. member make a suggestion as to how that could be accomplished?
Yes, very easily, by a system of taxation of land values.
Which system?

Any system which would take the economic rent of the land. That would mean that lands of that kind should be taxed when they are held out of use. It is the well known principle of the so-called single tax. I do not mean to carry out the full principle of the single tax, but if lands are held out of use, I say they should be more heavily taxed. If lands which are particularly valuable along the lines of railway, are held for speculative purposes, they should be more heavily taxed. The actual
bona fide settler is carrying the load, enhancing the value of these lands, and thus putting money into the pockets of the people who are doing no work on the land.	,

Would we require a special survey branch to find out what lands are in use and what are not in use? And if we carry out the principle the* hon. member suggests, would wTe not require this amount to be voted for the service?
Any real estate office will give the information required; or it could be obtained in the municipal offices.
Or from the Canada Colonization. Company.
Yes. What we need is a new policy.

Would the hon. member
suggest that the Dominion government should tax the lands in Canada or that the municipal go.vernment should do it?

Under present circumstances, the Dominion might well^ tax them, since they were originally Dominion lands intended for homestead purposes. But the original idea has been frustrated, and in a great many instances these lands that ought to belong to the homesteaders have been appropriated by private interests and are not now available for the real settlers, who have been induced to come here, and if possible to buy lands which ought to be granted freely to the people and which will need to be granted freely to the people if they are going to make a living on them.

speechtext:

taxation called the Wild Land tax, under which any land suitable for agriculture or growing purposes has to bear a special tax, and the results have been excellent. The speculator would either have to rent his land or sell it at a reduced price. Conditions are such in the western provinces that the tax

will compel many people to abandon the lands. If a person wants cheap land all he has to do is to go to the municipal clerk, and he can generally buy a very reasonably priced piece of land in a municipality for the taxes.

This work, I understand, has been going on for many years. Is it something that will continue for a good many years yet in Canada?

Direction
measurement is a continuation of the 1923 operations to extend the triangulation from Cape Breton island to Newfoundland, to serve as a basis for similar work in that country and to co-ordinate the charting of Newfoundland waters with that now being done in Canadian waters and that formerly done by the British Admiralty in the same district. One subparty will complete this work and then move to the Baie des Chaleurs where it will join the other sub-party to continue the St. Lawrence river triangulation along the Baie des Chaleurs and the east coast of New Brunswick.

. A secondary triangulation party will operate in the Fredericton, N. B. vicinity, establishing control points for the topographical survey mappers.

Another party is to control charting of that part of the gulf of St. Lawrence at present being charted by the Hydrographic Survey, to serve as a basis for provincial surveys north from the north shore of the gulf. That is the work that is being done in the Maritime provinces for this year.
Another survey is a continuation of the secondary triangulation which in 1922-23 was carried along the Upper Saguenay river, lake St. John and southward towards Three Rivers.
The 1924 operations will continue this work southward to connect with the primary triangulation near Three Rivers.
The statement which I have proceeds:
Ottawa river. This work is a continuation of the triangulation up the Ottawa river to serve as a basis for geographical work by the National Defence department and the Ontario and Quebec governments.
49th Parallel-Party No. 5 .. .. [DOT][DOT]	 $21,500
Continuation of primary triangulation along the international boundary from the 103rd meridian (near Estevan, Sask.) eastward to Lake of the Woods. The section from the 109th meridian to Lake of the Woods is the Canadian share of a co-operative scheme with the United States Coast and Geodetic Survey. The western half of the Canadian section has been completed. This net will form the basis of all future triangulation in western Canada.
British Columbia-Alberta Boundary-Party
No. 6	 514,400
The operations in this section are secondary triangulation to control the geographic position and accuracy of the boundary surveys from Yellowhead pass northwest to the intersection of the continental watershed with the 120th meridian.
In 1922 and 1923 the reconnaissance for the selection of stations was completed and almost one quarter of the angle measurement was finished. In 1924 four parties will be able to conclude the angle measurements and measure the base line at the north end of the section, thus completing the work.
British Columbia-Party No. 7	 $18,130
To furnish control for the hydrographic survey of the Department of Marine and Fisheries, the provincial government of British Columia, and to serve as a basis for surveys of all kinds.
Base Lines-Party No. 8	 $7,000
These base lines are measured at intervals in triangulation nets to check the scale of the triangulation so that the effect of the accumulation of angular measurements can be checked and corrected.
Four base lines are required during 1924, one in the northern British Columbia coast net, two on the 49th parallel net and one on the Ottawa river triangulation.
Geodetic Astronomy-Party No. 9	 $4,000
Geodetic astronomy consists of the establishing of Laplace points for the determination of astronomic longitudes and azimuths at triangulation stations of the geodetic survey to improve the accuracy of the work by eliminating the bend or twist that otherwise tends to develop in the triangulation.
The establishing of Laplace points is one of the most important phases of field astronomic work and is one of the most essential parts of the field work of the Geodetic Survey of Canada.	#
Six Laplace stations are required in 1924, two along the B.C.-Alberta boundary, three along the 49th parallel and one on the Ottawa river.
Precise Levelling-Parties No. 10 to 12. $20,000
This work is for the purpose of determining the elevations above mean sea level of points to serve as bases for surveys of all kinds.
