Is part of this vote to be used for building towers? If so, are the towers to be permanent structures?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These towers are for the purpose of taking very long observations.
But are they permanent structures?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are built of wood and will last the ordinary lifetime of wood.

I ask the question because about seven years ago one of these towers was built on a high hill within four miles of where I live. It was constructed of fir and spruce, the least durable of woods, and fell down a few years later. It must have cost a considerable sum of money as quite a large party was engaged in its construction, which occupied some time. To construct towers of such material is in my opinion simply a waste of money and labour, for they will last at best only three or four years. There is plenty of cedar in that country, and it would be more economical to use it in these towers.

Cedar is very scarce on
hilltops.
Mr. CAT,DWELL: But at the foot of hills there is cedar.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that these towers are now constructed in conjunction with the Forestry branch of the New Brunswick government and are of a much more permanent character.

The tower of which I am speaking was not built for forestry work, the district being devoted entirely to farming. I understand that to-day the government in New Brunswick is building look-out towers in
Supply-Interior

forest areas for fire protection service. My point is that it is a waste of energy and money to build towers of material so entirely lacking in durability.
Is it not a fact that once the geodetic survey is completed these towers are of no further use and may be taken down?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is
correct, except that now in most of the provinces wherever there are forest areas these towers are afterwards utilized for fire protection work, and therefore a little more care is being exercised in their construction. I think the tower in question was in use only two or three months.
It appears to me that we can save money on this geodetic survey. I notice that in 1918-19 according to the Estimates $112,000 was spent; in 1919-20, $149,000; in 1920-21, $290,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed that when the boundary survey was nearly completed a number of the men came into this department, which, with the returned soldier problem, accounts for the $290,000 voted in 1920-21. In 1922-23 the same condition prevailed. The work has expanded; there is no doubt about that. This year we are trying to get back to the old condition of affairs, and to that end we have cut off $50,000.

In 1921-22 there was an
item in the estimates of $37,000 for international boundaries, and in 1922-23 an amount of $35,000. They were in separate items, and they did not appear under the geodetic survey. In 1921-22 there was $325,000 for the geodetic survey and in 1922-23 a similar amount. In 1918-19 the amount was $112,000 and in 191920, $149,000. I think it is time we got back to the level,-back to the ground.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The reclassification of these services added a considerable amount to the expenditure. My hon. friend is referring to years when the service was perhaps at its lowest, following the period of the war. When a man moves out his position is not filled, and we are cutting down services as fast as we can without creating too great hardship. Not that I am asking that the government carry a group of men who are not rendering service; that is not my point at all. If these men had been continued on the day rate basis I do not think they would have had serious complaint to offer had their work been discontinued, but I think it is only fair to those men who were blanketed in in 1919 that we should proceed

as we are doing. Throughout the whole of the Interior department we are reducing the services as fast as we can, and I expect to reduce in the same way next year until we get back to where we were in 1916-17.

Last year there was no
reduction at all. We asked for a reduction and the minister told us pretty much what he is telling us now. After three or four years of high pressure he now takes off $50,000 That is no reduction at all; we are still double what we were in 1918-19 and 1919-20.

I notice in the Auditor
General's report that some men engaged in this work get a living allowance of so much per day and at the same time charge so much for board and lodging. I wonder if they can do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think I have in mind the case my hon. friend mentions. This man was brought here in 1921-

I did not have that particular case in mind, but as the minister has mentioned it I may be allowed to refer to it. In 1921 the Field Superintendent of Irrigation was brought from Calgary to Ottawa to perform special duties here. An order in council was passed on, I think, the 23rd of July, granting him a living allowance of $6 per day. In January, 1922, an order in council was passed granting him $1,086.50 to bring his family from Calgary to Ottawa. It is now over three years since he was moved from Calgary to Ottawa. He is permanently situated here, drawing his regular salary, and at the same time he is drawing this $6 living allowance. I would like to ask the minister if they can do that.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes, I will have to admit they can do that. The regulations provide that when you move a man from his headquarters you pay his removal expenses if he receives no increase in pay. We had a great many of these last year because we have been closing offices, moving men about and trying to cut down the staff with a view to economy. If there is an increase in pay the removal expenses are not paid. In this case, as I understand it-this happened before I came into the office-Mr. Peters was brought from Calgary in connection with the reorganization of the survey staffs. I am not denying that there have been difficulties in that connection and that things have not been as smooth as we would like in the reorganization work. Subsequent to his arrival here, after a very considerable delay a competition was arranged by the

Supply-Interior
Civil Service Commission and Mr. Shanks was given the position. As soon as this was brought to my attention the living allowance to Mr. Peters was stopped; that was some time about the middle of last summer. Mr. Peters is here, but he has drawn no living allowance since then. Mr. Shanks is confirmed in the position by the Civil Service Commission. Mr. Peters was up to the time of his removal here a permanent official of the Surveys branch, attached to the Irrigation branch at Calgary. I did not follow my hon. friend's question about living expenses.
On page K-179 of the Auditor General's report it is shown that Mr. Rannie is allowed $5 per diem for living expenses while at the same time he charges for lodging and board.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That is quite correct. There is provision for $5 a day when they are away from Ottawa on their inspection work.

The minister knows that Mr. Peters was drawing his regular salary and in addition to that drew a living allowance of $6 a day for over two years. Is that in the interests of economy? I think any man in the public service should be satisfied with one salary. One is sufficient, it seems to me, and I am sure the people would think so too. If the custom is otherwise, the quicker we stop it the better.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I agree
thoroughly with my hon. friend. There have been a good many cases in which delay has occurred, particularly with respect to removals and adjustments of this kind. I know of no case so long as that mentioned by my hon. friend, but I may cite one case of an agent being removed from Moose Jaw to Lethbridge. In that case it was over four months before he was confirmed in his position, and under the regulations we paid during that period a living allowance, just as we do to Mr. Rannie when he leaves his headquarters and goes out on inspectional work. We also pay the moving expenses if there is no increase in salary.

I would like to read the
last sentence of a letter from Mr. W. W. Cory, the deputy minister, in regard to this question:
In the meantime, however, until this is settled, I don't think he should be called upon to make any refund, on the contrary we should continue to pay the living allowance authorized by Council.

speechtext:
(Argenteuil):	I stopped
that living allowance at once.

If I caught the minister
correctly he said a moment ago that the living allowance of this gentleman, Mr. Peters, was cut off the middle of last year.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not the exact date, but it was some time last year. It was at the date that Mr. Shanks was confirmed in the position.

I am not referring to
that incident, but I am under the impression that in the Auditor General's report there is a letter from the Auditor General to the Treasury Board dated about the end of January of this year in which he objects to the continuance of this allowance being paid to Mr. Peters, but he waived further objection on the distinct understanding that Mr. Peters was immediately to go back to Calgary. It was something to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think I
am right about that.

The minister may be
right. I have not the Auditor General's report under my hand or I could read the letter. In any case a protest was made by the Auditor General on two or three occasions and finally he appealed to the Treasury Board, and the question which I think it is proper to ask the minister to explain is why the department persisted in continuing this man's living allowance in Ottawa when his services were certainly not required here for many, many months, and when it is doubtful if he should have been allowed to stay here for perhaps the last year under the circumstances. I do not wish to embarrass the minister too much. I know he has a lot to look after, the Post Office Department on top of his own, and perhaps it is unfair to expect him to know too much about his own department. It might be well to have a new Postmaster General to help him out in his labours. But I think it is wholly unfair to the country, and absolutely unwise from an administration standpoint to keep expensive officials comparatively idle, and when I say that I think I am speaking very, very kindly about this gentleman, and continuing to pay him a living allowance in addition to a very handsome salary over a period of-I have forgotten just how long but it was quite a long period, a year and a half or thereabouts. Furthermore, I think that when the Auditor General merely drew the minister's attention to the fact it should have been remedied at once, and the Auditor General should not have been forced to go to the Treasury Board and get a further ruling on the matter; and then only at the last
Supply-Interior

moment under a strict stipulation that the man should go at once out of the city and back to his former haunts was the payment authorized.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am sure
no living allowance has been paid him since October.

The minister is quite
sure of that?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am
taking the word of my official.

I do not question the
minister's sincerity, but I am a little doubtful of his accuracy.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My recollection of the circumstances is quite clear. When Mr. Shanks was confirmed in the position I at once gave instructions that the living allowance for this man was to be discontinued. As a matter of fact, I am not at all in sympathy with that sort of thing.

Do I understand the
minister to mean that he is continuing this service for the purpose of keeping certain men employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

I took that certainly
from what the minister said a few moments ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
After the
period of the war a large addition was made to the staff. I am not for one moment suggesting that this is not a valuable service, because I think it is, for all other survey work must commence from the work done by the geodetic survey. Neither am I making the excuse that we could not get along with perhaps less men, but I do ask the indulgence of the committee to allow me to cut down reasonably in this case as I did in the other. I have cut off $50,000 from this vote this year. I can say to my hon. friend that this is not work that deteriorates in value or is lost; it is very valuable work .
It is pointed out to me that a great many requests come to me for this work, and that is true. We are not able to satisfy perhaps 75 per cent of the requests we get for precise levelling and surveys along the shores for the purposes of navigation and charting. I can only plead with the committee to take a reasonable view of this matter. I am cutting this service just as fast as I think we should be warranted in doing, having in mind the service that has to be performed and the difficulties we have in cutting down the staff. This is not a service that has been inaugurated

since the war. Many of the men in this service enlisted, and when they returned from the war they expected to get their jobs back, and ail credit to the old government that gave them their jobs back. Now we have the responsibility of cutting down this staff, which includes many returned soldiers, and turning them adrift when there is little to do; but it will have to be done.

This is really a very important matter. A principle is involved. I do not doubt the minister's word for a moment, but it is possible that he is not as conversant with the details of his department as he might be. I think it would be well for me to read the letter of protest from the Acting Auditor General, dated December 13, 1923. He says:
Sir-On July 23rd, 1921, an Order in Council (P.C. 83/2614) was passed granting to Mr. F. H. Peters, Field Superintendent of Irrigation at Calgary, who was called to Ottawa to be temporarily assigned to special duties in the Department of the Interior, a living allowance from March 1st, 1921, of $6.00 a day while on special duty in Ottawa.
On January 31st, 1922 an Order in Council (P.C. 41/200) was passed authorizing the payment to Mr. Peters of the sum of $1,084.50 being the amount of his removal expenses from Calgary to Ottawa. From the accounts rendered in support of this claim Mr. Peters appears to have removed his family from Calgary to Ottawa in the early part of October, 1921.
Although Mr. Peters was paid his removal expenses nearly two years ago the Department of the Interior has continued to pay, and is still paying, the per diem allowance of $6.00 to Mr. Peters, on the grounds that he has not yet been permanently assigned to duties in Ottawa, but that he still holds the position of Field Superintendent of Irrigation with headquarters (nominally) at Calgary.
As the payment of this living allowance has been continued for such an extended period I should like to be informed if it was the intention of the Treasury Board that it should be paid so long as Mr. Peters was retained in Ottawa, notwithstanding the fact that his removal expenses were also paid some two years ago. The last official intimation that I have as to the payments to Mr. Peters makes the total amount of $5,850 paid him on account of living allowance up to October 31st, last, in addition to the $1,084.50 paid as removal expenses.
There is another letter here dated January 10, 1924 from Mr. J. C. Saunders, secretary of Treasury Board, which reads as follows:
Dear Sir,-I beg to acknowledge receipt of your communication of the 13th, ultimo, concerning continuation of per diem living allowance to Mr. F. H. Peters of the Department of Interior.
The Treasury Board, after full consideration of the special circumstances connected with this case, and in view of Mr. Peters' return to Calgary at an early date, are of the opinion that payment of his living allowance may be continued until his departure from Ottawa.
That is over three years ago and he is still drawing his $6 per diem according to this correspondence. I am sure the minister is not cognizant of the real situation.

The more I think it
over the less I like this vote, largely owing to the fact that I think it is not one of the essentials. That may be due to my ignorance of the character of the work that is carried on, or at least some of it. But in view of the fact that we have a big cut of $250,000 in connection with the Health of Animals Act, and another reduction of $50,000 in the estimates for the Health department, a very important one too having reference to combating venereal disease, and numerous others, it looks to me as if we are proposing here to spend too much money in non-essentials. That is my candid opinion as a member of the House. Then it must also be remembered that the grant for agricultural instruction to the provinces has been discontinued. In view of these facts I think the country at large will view expenditure of this kind with a great deal of disfavour. As members of parliament our object should be to cut out all the unnecessary frills at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In reply to my hon. friend I would just say that this is a basis for all survey work. It is the charting of our shore line. Most of this work, as hon. gentlemen know, is done in the East, but I am not offering that as any special reason why it should be continued. I agree with my hon. friend that unnecessary expenditure should be cut to the bone; but all survey work of every character, whether it is

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Supply-Interior

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: of a municipal or provincial character starts and hinges on these accurate points, and the very best engineers in the service are employed on this work. And indeed it is a most important one. If I had not inherited this work I could probably say to my hon. friend "Yes we can slash right and left." I think that in comparison with the cuts in the other votes I have not been backward. I have tried to cut the estimates of my department from one end to the other, sometimes in a very arbitrary way.

Does the minister contend that there is a large part of our coast line in the Maritime provinces that is not yet charted? If so what benefit to the charting of a coast line would the construction of these towers made of fir poles be? These towers are erected on the top of bald hills from which you can see twenty miles in any direction. The erection of such towers is rather a jbke to our people.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.

speechtext:
This man
was injured on the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway.
John Hedin was a section man in the employ of the T. and N.O. Railway and was injured on October 17, 1921, in a collision between our precise levelling party's motor car and a section motor car on which Hedin was riding. It has not been brought out that the accident was either party's fault-it was apparently an unavoidable occurrence.
The raihvay referred the case to the Workmen's Compensation Board of Ontario in the regular manner and they awarded Hedin the sum of $994.40 for medical and hospital services and loss of time, together with a pension of $20 per month for life for permanent partial disability.
)

The Department of Justice ruled on July 6, 1923, that our department was not liable under the terms of the agreement with the T. and N. O. Railway covering the operation of motor cars for precise levelling purposes.
Mr. Lee, the chairman of the T. and N. O. Railway Commission, urged however, that this department should reimburse the commission for the full amount of the award on the grounds of moral responsibility, since the accident would not have happened but for the presence of our party on the line. He also intimated that no further geodetic operations along the railway would be permitted until an adjustment of the matter, satisfactory to them, has been made. In view of the moral responsibility which undoubtedly exists and of the hindrance which would be caused to geodetic operations by the railway's refusal to allow same on their property, it has been considered proper that payment of the claim be arranged on other than legal grounds.

In fact, the suggestion is only an evidence of the fact that the person making it knew nothing whatever of the subject.

not because I have any objection to a population receiving necessary service simply because it is a sparse population scattered over a large country, but viewing all the other items that have been passed, the salaries and expenses in connection with it, the expenses of the council-and I am glad to have heard the explanation of how the expenditure is made up-the grant for roads, salaries for judicial administration, federal board, and all the other expenses that go with it, I was thinking that if this population continues to dwindle it is going to be expensive for us to maintain. But I am not opposing any such vote simply because the population is scanty. They are entitled to all the services that are necessary.

I would like to
make it quite clear to the hon. member that my remarks were not directed towards his question, but towards the idea that the administration of the Yukon Territory should be undertaken by the government of British Columbia.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: These supplies were placed on the S. S. Arctic. We leave policemen up in the north country throughout the whole of a very long winter, during which they see no white men till the Arctic returns and relieves them with two other men. We have three posts up there on the eastern coast of Canada. As my hon. friend knows there are exploring parties in there continuously. Indeed, we found a professor representing the Danish government up there who had spent three years on the southern end of Melville island. It might be said that perhaps this territory is not worth holding, but so far we have discovered very valuable deposits of coal up there, there may also be minerals and we thought it well to spend some money to maintain our sovereignty over that particular area. I thought I had a map here showing the posts. At all events, we have three posts up there, one at Pond's Inlet and two others, and we hope to establish two more on the eastern coast of Canada to look after the preservation of the game and enforce law and order among the native tribes to be found up there. These men, two in a company, remain up there during the whole winter season, and can only be visited during a very short time in the midsummer months. A ship will have to be sent there annually for that purpose. Last year, when this vote was under consideration, a judicial party had gone up in that country as far as Cumberland gulf to try a murderer. We had also to send a judicial party to the mouth of the Mackenzie river, to Aklavik, for the very same purpose, and we will have to send another party there this year. This may seem a considerable expenditure, but these are the outposts of civilization, they are expensive to reach, and can be reached only during a very limited time.
I presume the judicial party are drawing their salaries to maintain them?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Then why furnish them with these cigars and cigarettes? Let them buy their own. It is the already overburdened taxpayers of Canada who have to foot the bill. This is a small item, but there is a principle involved, and it runs all the way through. I think we cannot condemn it too strongly.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will remember that we are sending up there an official party representing the government of Canada. They meet other parties, representatives of foreign countries, and I do not think in view of the circumstances we have been over-extravagant in putting a few packages of cigarettes and some tobacco on board the ship for that purpose, but if we have I will see that it does not go this year.
Why not send men there who do not smoke?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The smokers buy their own tobacco.
Will the minister say that this is a justifiable expenditure?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Frankly, I have never heard of it before. I did not know they took these things, but I would not object to a reasonable amount of tobacco going with a party of that kind, officially representing the Canadian government as they do.
The minister thinks that is in the interests of economy?
If the cigarettes are good.

Is there any hope of any people ever living up there, or is there any possibility of ever digging out the coal or any mineral wealth that may be up there? I would not deny these men the pleasure of having a few cigars and cigarettes if they are meeting people in a friendly way, but is this expenditure to be continued year in and year out?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think it is wise for us to exercise some oversight over the Canadian tribes, because as my hon. friend knows, if you do not protect them, the traders, who are not particularly anxious about the welfare of the native Eskimo, get in amongst them and debauch them, carry in liquor and exercise an evil influence among the tribes, and then the responsibility is ours. The Eskimo problem is beginning to be a rather serious one for us to handle, and we are establishing police posts at various points along the coast to protect the Eskimo and preserve their game.
Supply-Interior

My observation is that instead of protecting the Eskimo we seem to be protecting the traders, or those who go in there. We try to enforce law and order among the Eskimos, who have never been trained along that line, and when they come into contact with the law they pay the extreme penalty whereas with their grey matter and mental development they are perhaps not able to appreciate justice in the same way that we do.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I had the pleasure of chatting with a trader who all last winter had been at Aklavik, where a' police post has been established for some time, and he told me that they carried on pretty much as people do on the outside, although it was dark all the time. They have gramophones, and some of the natives who have come in contact with civilization have their own fishing boats and they generally, according to his report, have a rather jolly time. I believe, and I think it is freely admitted, that the Eskimo lends himself much more rapidly to civilizing influences than do the tribes of Indians to be found north of the Great Slave lake and along the Mackenzie river.
This work will be continued year in and year out?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. That is to say the ship will have to visit these coasts. But we have been building houses, carrying in supplies and getting established. That work will not need to be done again.
The second item for establishing and operating wireless stations, including the erection of buildings and investigation work, and so forth, shows an increase of $55,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Last year
we established two wireless stations, one at Dawson and the other at Mayo in the Yukon. This brought about I think, a veiy considerable saving, particularly in the upkeep of lines and poles. This year we are establishing other wireless stations in the territories. We shall put in a central distributing station-I think that is decided now-to be located at Edmonton. We shall put in a station at Fort Vermilion, another at Fort Smith, and thus have a means of wireless commuiciation down the McPherson, eventually establishing a complete chain of communication with the far northern posts-with the posts along the Mackenzie river and with Mayo and Dawson, the chief distributing centre being Edmonton. So that throughout the whole of the north country, during the whole period of nine months in which it is shut up by the rigorous winter, the people will have some communication with the outside world.

Will this item include al!
the stations in the Northwest?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This includes Edmonton.
Does it include the whole of the stations?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

There is an item in this
vote for pensions?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I know to
what my hon. friend refers. When the Arctic was descending the St. Lawrence, after she left Quebec, she ran into a severe storm, and two of the seamen were drowned. There is a vote to provide an allowance for the widow and the relatives of the two men who were drowned on that occasion.
Will the minister explain what is the situation with respect to Wrangel island?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is not very much to explain. We have had a great deal of discussion with Mr. Stefansson with respect to Wrangel island. I cannot recollect just at what period this government informed him that they were not interested in Wrangel island as it lay off the coast of Siberia. But we had received information in a roundabout way that the British Admiralty might be interested in Wrangel island as a flying base. The reports were that British aviators might fly across the northern portion of Canada and on to the Orient. Stefansson went to England and interviewed the authorities there, but apparently the English government is not willing to set up any particular claim to Wrangel island, at least I have not heard that such is their intention. I do not know officially what they propose doing, but so far as Canada is concerned we do not intend to set up any claim to the island.

Has the government
made any investigation with respect to the death of the men who were left on the island?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, we
were not responsible for the expedition in any way.
This item makes provision for exploration does it not? Does that include the steamer Arctic?

speechtext: Yes.

Would the minister state just what the Arctic cost last year and what work was performed?

speechtext:
She went
on an expedition from Quebec into the Arctic circle taking a judicial party with her for the purpose of trying an Eskimo at Cumberland gulf, I think, and then on up to try to establish a post at Etah which would be the most northerly post that we have, or just opposite Etah on Melville island. However, the ice conditions did not permit her to land the material for this post and she was forced to return to the post established a year ago on the south of the island. She relieved the post there, visited the post at Pond's Inlet, then returned and picked up the judicial party and came back to Quebec.

Would the minister give

double bottom. The Arctic is an old ship, a very slow sailer, and. very expensive to send into that territory. Would the minister tell us at what time this expedition started from Quebec, and the probable date when it reached or tried to reach Melville island? I wanted to know what the ice conditions were so that I could understand the nature of the navigation in Hudson straits.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think I

At about what time?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If I remember rightly about the middle of July, I think about the 15th, of that month. She returned -I am not exactly sure of the date-about the last week in September.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have a
very clear map here. If my hon. friend is interested in it we will be able to show what happened. She attempted to reach the most northerly point we contemplated for a post but she was shut out by the ice. I hope my hon. friend is not thinking about the entrance to Hudson bay because that is many hundreds of miles south.
I should like to ask the minister if any other government, besides the Canadian government, have established posts on any of these northern island contiguous to Canada?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

And if they are making a
claim to sovereignty of any of these islands?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course
my hon. friend is aware that international law, in a vague sort of way, creates ownership of unclaimed lands within one hundred miles of any coast, even if possession has not been taken. At least there is a sort of unwritten law in that respect. Of course possession is a very large part of international lqw as well as any other law. But in this particular vicinity, at about the most northerly post we have established at the moment, in north of these islands, a Danish professor has been located for the past three years making investigations-not in any way, I imagine, attempting to establish sovereignty over these particular lands, or anything of that sort, but purely for scientific purposes, and that is the vicinity in which we found coal. In former days coal has been placed upon ships from that district, and it is not uncommon for whalers to be found there every year. That water is filled by ships from many parts of the world on whaling expeditions and trading expeditions as well; so that it is somewhat important that we should be established there.

Will the minister tell us why the discrimination or the differeilce in the compassionate allowance to the mother and to the widow? There may have been children. I never did like this word "compassionate." I never found a government admit any liability where there is any death. I have reference to a death which occurred on the Swift Current agricultural farm. If anything happens under anybody else's jurisdiction, it is not a "compassionate" allowance; the verdict is rendered by justice, or justice is satisfied. speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: Especially the half.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: On that basis I have been trying to economize as much as possible, but I have discovered that two inspectors cannot do the work. It is not our intention to completely close the three offices referred to; that is, any individual desirous of doing business will not have to travel any greater distance except in cases of leasing, as practically all the other work will be continued in those offices. Of course, complete records will be kept only at Moose Jaw and Prince Albert, so that transfers will have to be made at those centres. We will try to make the change operate as little as possible to the inconvenience of people living in the neighbourhood of Swift Current, Saskatoon and Battle-ford.

Are many homesteads
being taken up now? Would it not be*possible to drop this line of work and encourage the settlement of lands near the railways?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The department has not considered the advisability of cancelling these obligations, but the department will certainly not press people unduly for payment. There are hundreds of people who have paid up in full, and my hon. friend will readily see that it would be most unfair to them to give special consideration to those who have not paid. This work entails very considerable amount of correspondence, notices are sent out and1 records kept of all this business, whether we get a considerable revenue or not. I can say, however, that there is no intention on the part of the department to unduly press anyone for payment ,of his obligation.

There is a considerable difference between the pre-emption which has been paid for, and the one where the obligation remains undischarged at the present time. In the main the pre-emption which has been paid for was the better class of land. There are 72
many types of land in that area, and it is in the poorer area where these pre-emptions are not paid for. I would ask the minister to give serious consideration to the suggestion that the obligations on these lands be cancelled. The lands which are paid for are in the main the better class of land, and I am satisfied that many of the settlers on the poorer class of land will be unable to pay for them unless we have a pronounced period of prosperity, which does not seem likely in the near future. I would therefore urge upon the minister the advisability of cancelling at least the interest charges on these pre-emptions remaining unpaid at the present time.

I would call the minister's attention to the fact that in those areas where pre-emptions still remain unpaid for, you can buy land patented for much less money than what the department is charging for these pre-emptions, and it seems ridiculous to expect these people who have taken these pre-emptions to pay for their homesteads when they can buy land already under improvement for less money than the department is charging. I submit that the least the minister can do is to wipe out the interest charges against these lands and start afresh again, and I hope he will give that suggestion his serious consideration. There are in the West large blocks of land that have been set aside as forest reserves. This setting aside was done some years ago and since that time-in some cases owing to fire, and in other cases mainly through the action of the lumbermen-the areas contained in these reserves have been largely cleared of timber and are very suitable at the present time for agriculture. Many of these areas are situated close to the railway line and a number of requests are coming through-I have received a great many such requests at one time or another-from people who want to enter homesteads on these areas, but owing to the fact that they have been set aside as forest reserves these persons are not allowed to make entry. Only a short time ago I received a petition to be forwarded to the Minister of the Interior, signed by over two hundred men who wanted to enter homesteads on the forest reserves. I have forwarded this petition to the minister, and I should like to ask him now if any action is being taken to have these reserves opened up for homesteaders?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Let me first say to my hon. friends, lest I forget it, that I can assure them of a very sympathetic consideration, but I think they will appreciate the difficulty the department is faced with in dealing with this problem. It may lateT on result in having a revaluation made, or some consideration being given to interest charges, before we clear this matter up, but I should like it to be borne in mind that we have the same difficulty to-day that we have in connection with the Soldier Settlement Board. Although some men have paid others have not paid. True, some of them are on inferior land and that fact perhaps might be given consideration. However, I can promise my hon. friends that I am prepared to give those men who have pre-emption and have heavy payments accrued against them very generous consideration.
With respect to the matter of returning to settlement lands set aside for forest reserve, here again you have a somewhat difficult question. If you allow settlement to get close to the vicinity of forest areas, where it is hoped to propagate and continue forest growth, you at once establish a somewhat dangerous menace to the forest itself. However, I am convinced that there is any quantity of inferior lands upon which timber can be grown and propagated without retaining any very considerable area of good agricultural land within the forest reserve. Wherever cases of this kind come up we 
conduct an investigation. Here again we find there are men who differ so widely in their reports that it sometimes takes a considerable time before we can decide to open up an area of such a character. However I can promise my hon. friend the most careful consideration of this request. I have before me now an investigation which is being made.

I should like to point out
that in some cases the lands are located along railway tracks, and there should not be any more danger from fire in connection with a homesteader than arises from the operation of trains. The very fact that these lands are near a railway, I think, should entitle this request to receive special consideration because an awkward situation arises when homesteaders take up land in outlying districts where no railway communication exists.

speechtext:
In the

I cannot
tell my hon. friend that.

I believe I am correct in stating that the figures of the Revelstoke office exceed any of the other two points. The figures at Revelstoke have increased each year since the office was opened in 1914. The revenue has greatly exceeded the expenditure at the Revelstoke office. It would look to me, if you are going to work it out on a question of economy, that you would have the office maintained at Revelstoke, which is the largest revenue paying office in the province. It is also at a point where there are more timber limits particularly adjacent to most of the business that is being done.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
My hon.
friend will notice that the revenues are almost upon an equality at Kamloops and Revelstoke; but the report we received here was that the one office would be quite sufficient to serve that particular locality, giving such service as might be necessary to the old points at which these offices were established. But one of the difficulties, of course, in trying to save money on administration is that no matter where you go with an office, or 
where you take away a service, it can easily be proven that it was very valuable to that community and that all the offices are needed.

In that connection, if
this particular office had not been a very good revenue producing office, there would have been occasion to have it moved or amalgamated as a matter of economy; but this office is right in the heart of the timber belt. All the timber and land business practically is controlled and has been controlled from Revelstoke. By moving that office from Revelstoke to Kamloops, you put the people of that particular district at a double inconvenience and you disorganize work that has been established for some few years and established on a very good basis. If it could be shown by checking the reports that this office had not been paying, I do not believe there would have been quite as much objection raised to its removal. far as my point is concerned. I did not want to ask the minister any unfair question, but he will know his predecessors in office have always taken a certain stand in regard to the proceeds from those pre-emptions.

I just want to elicit from
the minister whether he is taking the same stand. I will not press the question; but I would like to remind the House at this juncture that the amendments to the Dominion Lands Act which created these pre-emptions and purchased homesteads were enacted by this House with the express purpose of supplying a fund for the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. Perhaps I shall be in order in just briefly reviewing what took place some years ago. The Dominion Lands Act of 1882, as I think is well known, made provision for building the Hudson Bay railroad. It provided a grant of 6,400 acres per mile for that part of the railroad reaching to the Saskatchewan river, and one grant of 12,800 acres per mile for that part reaching from the Saskatchewan river to the bay. Part of that grant was subsequently earned by a private company, that part relating to the road up to the Saskatchewan river. The other pari of the grant was left in abeyance until 1906. At that time, due to the influx of immigrants into Saskatchewan and Alberta, the question of the Hudson Bay road became vital once more, and both political parties then acknowledged the rights of the West with regard to the construction of that railroad. It became a plank in the platforms of both political parties, and the Liberal government at that time, coming to a fresh lease of power, acknowledged that right to the furthest extent.
I feel the hon. member is hardly in order at this particular time.

When I came into the House
a short while ago, these pre-emptions and homesteads were being discussed, and I am dealing with the proceeds of the sales of those pre-emptions and homesteads.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I thought the hon.
member was dealing more particularly with the Hudson Bay railway than with pre-emptions and homesteads, if I am not mistaken.

I am leading up to a question.
I am afraid that the minister will not be able to give a very intelligent answer to my question unless I outline the situation. I was about to say that the Liberal government at that time, through the hon. gentleman's predecessor, thought fit to amend the Dominion Lands Act in this regard. The alleged reason for the amendment was twofold: to bring the act up to date and also to incorporate in it the principle which the Liberal party had adopted, that of "no land grants to railways." When Mr. Oliver proceeded to do that, he found himself in a dilemma. To do away with land grants to railways looked like going back on the West with respect to the Hudson Bay railway. His ingenuity was exercised considerably in order to get over that, and the pre-emption clause with which we are dealing to-night was the result. Mr. Oliver brought forth that amendment providing for the purchase of homesteads and pre-emptions in order to get over that difficulty, and he got over the difficulty to some extent. If it did away with grants to railways, thus carrying out the Liberal principle of "no land grants to railways," at the same time it made ample provision for the Hudson Bay railroad. That is the point I want to draw to the attention of the minister, the government and this House to-night, namely that the proceeds realized and to be realized from those purchased homesteads and pre-emptions with which we are dealing to-night, are, morally speaking, the property of the West in respect of the building of the Hudson Bay railroad. That is the situation that has always been acknowledged in this House. When Mr. Oliver was bringing this legislation before the House, he iterated and reiterated this fact: that the sole object in bringing in this legislation was to provide for building the Hudson Bay railroad; that there was no other object. He went so far as to say that if the provision alone was not sufficient to complete the road, he would make it sufficient; he would contribute land in order that sufficient money might be realized for the purpose of com-
Supply-Interior

pleting the railway to the bay. I thought 1 would take advantage of this opportunity to bring that before the House and the government in order to revive in the minds of the people at the present time the fact that the W est has in this respect a right that has always been acknowledged, that never at any time has been questioned and that is wTitten large upon the pages of Hansard, both at that time and since. Without pressing the minister to declare his attitude in the matter, I shall be content with placing that fact before the House.

I should like to make a plea to the minister for leniency in regard to those who have leased grazing lands at a very high price. To-night we have learned that some grazing lands have been leased for two cents an acre, and in some cases, the price has been 20 cents an acre and more. Grazing land leased at 20 cents an acre a few years ago when times were good, was all right, but the price of stock having gone down, it is quite apparent that 20 cents an acre is an exorbitant price. I have a case in mind at the present time of a party who has spent a considerable amount of money on grazing land in building fences and who is now in arrears. I might point to a case which came up either last session or the session before, where in the sale of a pulpwood berth in the northern part of Manitoba, I believe, a concession was given by the minister to those who had made the purchase on the ground that the price had been too high. I cannot remember all the details, but that is what took place. Will the minister follow the same course and deal leniently with those who have purchased or leased grazing lands at the high price of 20 cents and even, I believe, 30 cents an acre?

speechtext: Were those Indian lands?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Of course they are in an altogether different category from Crown lands, and unfortunately during the period of the war some very high figures were paid for grazing lands, in some cases in Alberta as high as 30 cents an acre. The hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) will,
I think, bear me out in the fact that this has broken two of the ranchers there. The matter is a very difficult one to adjust. I Mr. Bird.]

I wish to repeat a request which I made to the minister last year. I quite anticipate that I shall receive the same reply, but the request is on behalf of individuals who have been given the .privilege of taking land in forest reserves. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) cited a similar case in his constituency. These men after settling there, persuaded themselves that they required a school district. Many of those lands have returned to the Crown, and the school districts in question are very hard pressed because of assessments and taxation which they are obliged to make in order to maintain their schools. I believe they have repeatedly requested the department, and I have received many requests to present their case on the floor of the House, to ask the Dominion government to assume the taxation on those lands that have reverted to the Crown. I,t seems to me logical to ask that in order to assist school districts which were constituted largely as a result of settlers going in there.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend is putting up a very difficult proposition to the department, for it would open the door very wide for innumerable claims, particularly on lands under the control of the Soldier Settlement Board throughout the whole of western Canada, and in the East too I presume. I am entirely in sympathy with his plea, but if the Crown undertook to pay taxes in such cases I do not know where it could stop.*
I wish-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: What the hon. gentleman is discussing should come under the fifth item-Protection of timber, tree culture, protection and management of forest reserves, surveys of forest resources and research in forestry and forest products and so forth.

I thought contingencies might < elate to the point as well. But I would direct the minister's attention to vote 141, the third item, "Halifax, Bellevue building- local improvement taxes, $1,777.77." I wonder if there is a differentiation between urban and rural taxes. Again I would remind the minister that the natural resources of Saskatchewan are retained by the federal government. Consequently it seems to me that our argument is stronger than the reference made to the eastern provinces, which own their natural resources.

I would direct the minister's attention to Indian and school lands

which were sold during the war at prohibitive prices. I understand that the interest rate in many cases was raised to 7 per cent when the purchasers did not keep up their payments. This has been a great hardship, especially as the value of products, from the farm, has gone down considerably, thus placing these men at a great disadvantage in keeping up their payments. Has the minister considered reducing the rate to, say, 6 per cent, to make it a little easier for them to meet their interest obligations?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The increase was made some four or five years ago at the request of the provincial governments. I believe I was one of the delegates who appeared before the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), then Minister of the Interior. Saskatchewan was perhaps most insistent at the time in making this request. We were asking that the school lands be turned over to us for administration purposes. It was pointed out to us that the function of the department was that of trustee for the provinces, and by special arrangement the interest rate was increased. If we have not already done so we intend to write to the provincial governments asking them to revert to the old rate of interest in order to relieve the situation somewhat. It is a matter in regard to which we must receive the consent of the provincial governments before we take action.
Would that include school as well as Indian lands?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: This item is hardly correct In order that when we come to discuss the vote hon. members will be aware exactly how it should stand, I would ask that an amending motion be made by my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power).

I move that item 13 be amended by inserting after the word "salaries" the words "including W. Ide, superintendent of staff, at $4,200." speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Excise
speechtext: Mr. Ide's name was in the estimates as submitted to be printed, but through some error it was omitted. Reference to page 83 will show that the amount is set out in the twelfth line, "superintendent, staff $4,200." It does not increase the estimate at all. I have taken this procedure because last year the same thing happened when the estimates of the Post Office Department were before the committee. The name of Mr. Anderson had been omitted, and a similar motion was made to rectify the mistake, I was the mover of the motion when my friend the present Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) was acting for the Postmaster General.

I do not object at all to my hon. friend moving the motion, but I would direct attention to an incident that occurred the other day when we were discussing certain items. A motion was made by an hon. member on this side of the House directing where the vote should go. It was ruled out of order on the ground that it was not competent far a private member to move such a motion, that it ought to come from a minister of the Crown. If the rule then was applicable to a private member on this side of the House, it would be equally applicable now to the hon. member for Quebec South.

speechtext:
A message has been received from the Senate informing this House:
That the Senate doth unite with the House of Commons in the approval of the convention between His Majesty and the President of the United States of America, signed at Washington on the twenty-third day of January, one thousand nine hundred and twenty-four, for the purpose of avoiding any difficulties which might arise between them in connection with the laws in force in the United States on the subject of alcoholic beverages, a copy of which has been laid before parliament, by inserting in the said resolution m the blank space therein the words "Senate and".
